name: Wooden waggonway
kb: Wooden or cast iron rails in a groove for wheels
note: Wheels with flanges to stay on track are less efficient than flanged rails with flat wheels. Medieval coal mines used L-shaped cast iron rails; wheels rode on top. The innovation is that grooved track keeps wheels from falling off without a separate flange.

name: Flanged cast iron wheel
kb: Cast iron wheel with projecting flange on one side
note: Flange on the wheel instead of groove in the rail lets wheels run on flat top rail. Requires casting tolerances within a few mm and case hardening to resist wear. The flange does slip sideways on curves if track is truly flat; banked curves help.

name: Edge rail in wrought iron
kb: Wrought iron rail with a thin raised edge for the wheel flange to run on
note: Wrought iron rail with vertical edge section for wheel flanges. Edge rail wears down from flange contact. Surveyors discovered that a thin raised iron edge on flat rail is better than thick cast iron rails; the wrought iron is softer and easier to shape, but wears faster.

name: Rail rolling in mill
kb: Passing heated bulk steel through rollers to form rail profile
note: Rolling mill produces consistent rail profile at tonnage scale. Early mills had to trial many roller shapes. The kernel is controlling the speed and temperature of the steel through multiple passes without cooling too much; too cold and the mill clogs, too hot and the steel deforms unevenly.

name: Bullhead rail
kb: T-shaped rail with bulbous head resisting vertical wear
note: Bulbous head can be turned over once worn on one side; reversible rail doubles its service life. Requires close-tolerance rolling and special chairs to clamp the head.

name: Flat bottom rail
kb: T-shaped rail resting on flat base seated directly on sleeper
note: Flat bottom rail sits directly on sleepers without chairs, saving weight and labour. Introduced after 1850 when rolling tolerances improved. The kernel is that the flat base distributes load better than a pointed foot, and eliminates the need for expensive cast iron chairs if sleepers can be accurately spaced.

name: Rail welding
kb: Electric arc or gas flame welding of rail ends into continuous long rail
note: Welded rail eliminates joints, reducing noise and wheel impact loading. Thermal stress during cooling must be controlled or the weld cracks. The kernel is that you must preheat the rail before welding, weld under careful arc control, then cool slowly in a lagging blanket. Uncontrolled cooling fails within weeks.

name: Fishplate for rail joining
kb: Wrought iron plate bolted over two rail ends to join them
note: Simple wrought iron plate on both sides of rail joint, bolted through. Prevents vertical deflection and twisting at the joint. The kernel is that bolted joints are maintenance-intensive because vibration loosens bolts; springs under bolt heads help, but regular tightening is essential.

name: Sleeper and ballast foundation
kb: Timber sleepers on stone ballast distributing rail load
note: Sleepers must be set at precise spacing and depth for even rail height. Ballast size matters: too large and rails rock, too small and it settles too quickly. Track workers use a wooden gauge and a line to check alignment.

name: Chair and key for bullhead rail
kb: Cast iron saddle clamping bullhead rail to sleeper with removable wedge
note: Chair sits on sleeper, the bulbous head of the rail slides into the chair, a wooden wedge or key is driven in to lock it. The kernel is that cast iron chairs can be removed and reused; cheaper than welding and allows track realignment. Keys must be replaced when they loosen.

name: Points and frog
kb: Movable rails and crossing point where two tracks meet
note: A frog is where two rails cross; a diamond-shaped casting with a gap in the middle. Points are two curved rails that slide together to guide wheels left or right. The kernel is that the frog must support wheels rolling through the gap at speed without bouncing; cast iron frogs crack unless cooled carefully. The angle between crossing rails is critical; too steep and wheels derail.

name: Locomotive turntable
kb: Rotating platform on central pivot for turning locomotives end-for-end
note: Central pivot must support a locomotive and distribute its weight through ball or roller races. The kernel is that a flat bearing surface with rolling elements is essential; a simple pivot fails under the oscillation of a heavy moving locomotive. Early turntables had crude bearings that required frequent greasing and re-packing.

name: Sprung coupling buffer
kb: Spring-loaded buffer between coupled vehicles absorbing impact
note: Buffers are rubbing plates; springs inside the coupler absorb the impact of coupling. Without buffers, sudden jerks break couplings and cargo. The kernel is that springs must not be too stiff or they waste energy heating up, not too soft or the buffer compresses too far and gets stuck.

name: Screw coupling
kb: Hand-screw coupling joining wagons by threaded hook
note: Two hooks with threaded rods; screwman walks between wagons turning the rod to couple them. Slow and dangerous. The kernel is that this requires discipline and exact position; if chains are too short, screwmen get crushed, if too long, wagons collide.

name: Automatic knuckle coupler
kb: Self-engaging hook-and-latch coupler closing on impact
note: Knuckle is a hinged hook; when two couplers touch, the spring-loaded knuckles close on each other. Eliminates the need for screwmen between wagons. The kernel is that the latching geometry must be precise enough that it does not pop open under oscillation, and hard enough to survive millions of couplings without rounding off.

name: Vacuum brake
kb: Partial vacuum in pipe pulls piston in brake cylinder applying all brakes
note: Brake pipe runs the length of the train; a pump on the locomotive creates vacuum. If any coupling breaks, air leaks in and brakes lock on all wagons instantly. The kernel is that vacuum is unreliable; brake cylinders weep, couplings leak, and the vacuum pump must run continuously. Westinghouse air brake is more reliable.

name: Westinghouse air brake
kb: Compressed air in pipe applies brakes; loss of air releases brakes
note: Westinghouse added a triple-valve: a mechanism that automatically applies brakes on each wagon when line pressure drops. No vacuum pump needed, just a compressor on the locomotive. The kernel is the triple-valve; loss of pressure in the main line triggers individual car brake application through the auxiliary reservoir on each wagon. This was revolutionary.

name: Bogie truck with leading wheels
kb: Four-wheel swiveling truck supporting front or rear of locomotive
note: Bogie is a small truck with four wheels; swivels on a central pin. Distributes weight over many wheels, reducing rail stress. The kernel is the pivot: it must allow the bogie to rotate for curves but cannot have play or the wheels will hunt side-to-side and derail. Friction damping is essential.

name: Leading truck for guiding
kb: Smaller four-wheel truck ahead of driving wheels for steering
note: Leading truck follows the curves because it leads; driving wheels follow the leading truck path. Without it, a long rigid wheelbase derails on curves. Much simpler than a bogie and works fine for short locomotives.

name: Locomotive boiler with multitubular flues
kb: Horizontal cylindrical vessel with many small tubes for hot gases
note: Dozens of small tubes in a large pressure vessel for heat transfer. Tube failures rupture the boiler explosively; ferrule expansion is standard.

name: Blastpipe for draught
kb: Exhaust steam nozzle in chimney creating suction on the firebox
note: Blastpipe is a small nozzle of steam in the chimney. Exhaust steam velocity creates low pressure, pulling hot gases through the firebox and tubes. Without it, a locomotive boiler makes barely enough steam to move itself. The kernel is this simple: a jet of steam pulls the fire. Diameter and shape matter; too tight and back-pressure rises, too loose and draught fails.

name: Superheater
kb: Additional tubes carrying steam through the hot gas stream
note: Superheater tubes run through the furnace smoke box; steam passing through is heated above saturation temperature. Dry steam has much better expansion efficiency and does not condense in the cylinders. The kernel is that if steam reaches saturation again in the cylinders from pressure drop, water slugs damage the valves and pistons; superheat prevents this.

name: Injector feedwater pump
kb: Steam jet drawing cold water into boiler against pressure
note: An injector uses a steam jet to entrain and accelerate cold water into the boiler against steam pressure. No moving parts; only valve adjustments. The kernel is that this is counterintuitive: steam at high pressure should push water out, not in. The trick is that the steam jet accelerates the water faster than the boiler pressure can push back.

name: Slide valve for steam distribution
kb: Flat plate sliding on ports to admit and exhaust steam in cylinders
note: Slide valve is a flat rectangular casting sliding back and forth on a flat plane. Ports in the plane align with slots in the valve to admit steam to cylinders and exhaust to atmosphere. The kernel is that it is simple and works, but creates a lot of friction because it is pressed hard onto the plane by steam pressure. Piston valves are an improvement.

name: Piston valve
kb: Cylindrical piston with ring ports moving inside a steam chest
note: A cylinder with ports in the side moves inside a steam chamber. Rings create sealing; ports on cylinder and chamber walls align to direct steam. Much lower friction than slide valve because only the seal rings contact the cylinder. Requires good machining and ring materials that do not gall.

name: Stephenson link motion
kb: Rocking link arm combining two eccentrics to control valve opening
note: A curved link arm rocks back and forth; two eccentrics (off-center cams) are attached at its ends. A rod from the link drives the valve. By moving the link up and down, you change which eccentric drives the valve, reversing the locomotive or adjusting cut-off. The kernel is that this is a pure mechanical function generator: no calculation needed, just mechanical linkage geometry that engineers discovered through trial.

name: Walschaerts valve gear
kb: Eccentric and crosshead combination for precise valve timing
note: Walschaerts uses the main piston rod as input to a linkage that drives the valve. The motion is more nearly sinusoidal than Stephenson, and the geometry allows rapid cut-off. Later discovered to be better than Stephenson. The kernel is that taking valve motion from the main piston rod instead of a separate eccentric is mechanically elegant and gives better speed control.

name: Compound expansion engine
kb: Two cylinders: high pressure first, then low pressure from exhaust
note: High-pressure steam in small cylinders expands, then exhausts into larger low-pressure cylinders. Receiver cooling improves efficiency.

name: Articulated locomotive
kb: Two or more sets of driving wheels with separate boilers or joined at the boiler
note: Articulated locomotives have a pivot at the center, allowing the rear unit to rotate for curves. Two sets of cylinders pulling one boiler. The kernel is the pivot and steam pipes: the feedpipes to rear cylinders must flex or the pivot motion will rupture them. Modern articulated designs use flexible pipes and careful geometry to manage stress.

name: Electric locomotive with trolley pole
kb: AC or DC electric motor drawing power from overhead or rail
note: Electric motors have better efficiency and control than steam. AC motors require substations; DC motors require heavy feeders from a central station. The kernel is that electric traction needs infrastructure investment in poles or conduits, but eliminates the boiler. Early systems used DC; AC came later with better transformers.

name: Third rail power conductor
kb: Copper or steel rail beside tracks conducting power
note: Third rail is at ground or low height beside the track. A shoe on the vehicle contacts it for power. Simpler than overhead catenary, but third rail gets dirty and the shoe wears. The kernel is that contact pressure and shoe material determine the electrical connection quality; insufficient pressure or worn shoes arc and cause voltage drop.

name: Overhead catenary for power
kb: Suspended cable overhead for pantograph to contact
note: Catenary wire sags naturally; a support cable above compensates for sag. Pantograph wheel rolls on the contact wire. The kernel is maintaining contact at speed: if the wire is too high the pantograph lifts off, if too low it sags into obstacles. Tension is maintained by weights on the suspension ends. Modern catenary uses elaborate linkages to keep tension constant as the wire stretches and temperature changes.

name: Pantograph current collector
kb: Articulated arm pressing a wheel or blade against overhead wire
note: Pantograph is a diamond-shaped linkage pushing a wheel up against the overhead wire. Spring pressure controls contact force. The kernel is that the wheel must not bounce off at speed, but excessive pressure increases wear and copper consumption. The contact strip is made from a copper alloy that conducts well but does not arc-weld itself to the catenary.

name: Diesel electric transmission
kb: Diesel engine driving an electrical generator, motor drives wheels
note: Diesel engine inefficient at low speed; generator produces electrical power, electric motor drives wheels. Electric transmission allows smooth power delivery.

name: Semaphore signal
kb: Mechanical arm with positions indicating proceed, caution, or stop
note: Semaphore arm at different angles means go, stop, or caution. All-night operation required lamps. The kernel is that a driver must know the state from a distance. Early railroad signals were simply 'stop' or 'go'; caution required a second signal to warn that the next signal might be red.

name: Block signalling system
kb: Dividing track into blocks, only one train per block
note: Track is divided into blocks; a signal at the entrance shows whether the block is occupied. Signalmen receive messages from block to block. The kernel is that this prevents rear-end collisions automatically: if a train fails to stop at a signal, it has already entered the block, so the signal behind is set to stop. The system requires discipline and communication between all signal boxes.

name: Track circuit for detection
kb: Electrical circuit through the rails detecting presence of train
note: A low voltage circuit is sent down one rail through a relay to the other rail. Train wheels and axles short the circuit, stopping relay current. The relay releases, changing the signal. The kernel is that this is fail-safe: if a wheel falls off, or a rail breaks, the circuit opens and the signal shows stop. No human can override it.

name: Interlocking for signal control
kb: Mechanical or electrical locking preventing conflicting switch and signal combinations
note: Interlocking prevents a signalman from throwing a switch that would cause a train to derail or collide. Early systems were mechanical: levers moved in sequence, and a mistake locked the lever. Later systems use electrical logic through a relay bank. The kernel is that the logic must be physically embodied, not trusted to human memory.

name: Automatic train stop
kb: Automatic alarm or brake activation if signal is passed at danger
note: A ramp or arm on the track activates a release or brake if the locomotive passes a stop signal. Driver hears a loud alarm and can take over. If the alarm is ignored, the brake applies automatically. The kernel is that this is the only purely automatic safety: all other safeguards require human adherence. Some systems use electromagnets; others use mechanical trip arms.

name: Sleeping car for passengers
kb: Passenger car with bunks for sleeping during overnight journey
note: Sleeping cars have bunk beds stacked vertically for economy, and superior suspension for ride comfort. The kernel is that passengers need privacy for sleeping; compartment design is essential. Early sleeping cars were dangerous if a coupling broke; springs and buffers improved safety.

name: Refrigerated wagon
kb: Insulated wagon with ice chambers preserving perishable cargo
note: Insulation is cork, sawdust, or felt in the walls. Ice chambers are at roof corners, cold sinks to preserve cargo. Air circulation must be designed carefully: stagnant cold spoils, circulating cold prevents moisture. The kernel is that predictable ice consumption and maintenance of air exchange are essential; a poor design spoils cargo before it reaches market.

name: Hopper wagon for bulk minerals
kb: Open wagon with conical bottom and chutes for gravity unloading
note: Hopper wagons eliminate shoveling; load coal or ore, close the chute, and gravity empties it at the destination. Chutes must be wide enough that cargo bridges; a stuck chute is worthless. Hinged chutes that open suddenly can jam if a stone wedges in the opening.

name: Tank wagon for liquids
kb: Cylindrical pressure vessel on wagon chassis
note: Tank wagons must be strong enough to support their own weight plus contents at speed over rough track. Seams must not leak; early tanks used hand-riveted seams prone to failure. The kernel is that a full tank at 60 tonnes bounces on rough track; suspension must be robust or the tank bends and ruptures.

name: Marshalling hump yard
kb: Hill over which wagons roll downslope into classification tracks
note: A train is uncoupled at the top, pushed over the hump by a small engine, wagons roll downslope and are switched into classification tracks by remote control. No manual switching needed. The kernel is calculating the gradient and friction so wagons roll at the right speed: too fast they collide, too slow they stop midway. Retarders (friction devices) on tracks control speed.

name: Clinker planking hull construction
kb: Overlapping hull planks fastened edge to edge
note: Each plank overlaps the one below; fastened with iron rivets or treenails. Flexes with the hull movement. The kernel is that overlap provides some hydrodynamic benefit at speed, and the joint overlaps create a labyrinth that slows leaking. Clinker hulls are lighter and more flexible than carvel.

name: Carvel planking hull construction
kb: Edge-to-edge hull planks fastened to internal frames
note: Planks meet edge to edge on the outside; frames inside hold the shape. Smoother hull than clinker, better for large vessels. The kernel is that seams must be perfectly caulked or the ship leaks. The planks are attached to frames with treenails (wooden pegs) or iron bolts; treenails are preferred because iron rusts and weakens the hull.

name: Frame-first hull construction
kb: Building the skeleton frame first, then planking
note: Medieval ships built shell-first, laying planks then adding frames. Renaissance builders discovered frame-first: build the ribcage, then plank. Allows precise shape and stronger hulls. The kernel is that frame-first needs accurate geometry; shell-first is intuitive but shapes are imprecise and hulls weaker.

name: Sternpost rudder
kb: Flat rudder hinged on the sternpost, directly below the helm wheel
note: Rudder is a flat board pivoting on iron gudgeons. Tiller arm connected to wheel sheaves and rope. The kernel is that medieval steering oars were inefficient; a post-mounted rudder has much better control. Larger rudders are essential at speed.

name: Lateen sail
kb: Triangular sail with leading edge parallel to the wind
note: Lateen sail hangs from a yard at an angle; the luff (leading edge) can point higher into the wind than square sails. Allows sailing across wind and returning. The kernel is that this is geometry: a triangular sail pointing into wind generates lift just as an airfoil does. Medieval sailmakers did not understand the physics, but found that this sail works.

name: Square rig sails
kb: Sails perpendicular to mast running with wind from behind
note: Square sails are powerful with wind behind you, useless when sailing toward the wind. Multiple sails on multiple masts allow some directional control. The kernel is that larger sail area means better speed, so sailing ships carried many sails and took time to adjust them in changing wind.

name: Fore-and-aft rig
kb: Sails aligned with the ship length controlled by a boom
note: Fore-and-aft sails point along the ship length. A boom extends below the sail, controlled by rope blocks. This rig allows sailing close to the wind. The kernel is that controlling the boom requires skill and strength; an accidental jibe (boom swing) can decapitate a sailor. Modern fore-and-aft rigs use mechanical systems to prevent that.

name: Jib triangular foresail
kb: Small triangular sail in front of the main mast
note: Jib hangs from a stay line forward of the mast. Small and easy to furl. The kernel is that removing the jib improves balance when the ship heels; jibs are the first sail doused in heavy weather.

name: Staysail
kb: Small triangular sail on a stay between masts
note: Staysails are rigged on the cable stays between masts. They fill the gap between main and jib. The kernel is that each small sail is easier to handle than one large sail, and distributes pressure to multiple parts of the rigging rather than concentrating loads on one sail.

name: Reefing sails
kb: Reducing sail area by rolling or folding part of the sail
note: Sailors work aloft on the yard rolling the sail and lashing it with reef points. Dangerous and slow. The kernel is that this is the only way to reduce sail in heavy weather without dropping it entirely; reef points must be strongly secured so the sail does not unfurl.

name: Capstan for hauling
kb: Vertical rotating post with rope wrapped around hauling cargo
note: Capstan has a vertical axle on a sturdy base; rope is wrapped and sailors push bars to rotate it. Mechanical advantage is excellent: one turn around the capstan multiplies force. The kernel is that rope can slip if tension is uneven; capstan bars must be moved by sailors in synchronized rhythm, or the rope loosens.

name: Windlass for anchor hauling
kb: Horizontal rotating drum hauling anchor cable
note: Windlass has gears reducing speed and increasing torque. Necessary for hauling heavy anchors against water pressure. The kernel is that gear reduction is essential: without it, even muscle power cannot raise an anchor in deep water. Early windlasses were hand-crank; later versions used steam power.

name: Block and tackle pulley
kb: Pulley blocks in series multiplying rope mechanical advantage
note: Multiple pulleys in wooden blocks distribute rope friction. A six-part tackle gives a six-fold mechanical advantage. The kernel is that each pulley adds weight and friction, so very large tackles lose efficiency; four to six parts is typical.

name: Chain cable
kb: Wrought iron chain for anchor cable replacing hemp rope
note: Chain cable is much stronger than rope, does not rot, and does not chafe. Requires chain windlass or capstan to handle weight. The kernel is that chain links must be perfectly closed or they open under cyclic load; link welding must be perfect or the chain fails suddenly.

name: Stockless anchor
kb: Anchor with hinged flukes no rigid stock bar
note: Flukes rotate on a pin, so anchor stows flat on deck. Older anchors had a rigid stock bar perpendicular to flukes; that required complex rigging to haul and stow. The kernel is that hinged flukes must seat reliably into the seabed; geometry must be exact or the anchor does not set.

name: Copper sheathing for wooden hulls
kb: Thin copper sheet covering hull below waterline
note: Copper is expensive but prevents marine growth (barnacles, weed) that increases drag. Needs copper nails for fastening; iron nails corrode and weaken the sheathing. The kernel is that copper is sacrificial: it oxidizes and protects the wood. Replacement is expensive but hull speed is preserved.

name: Caulking with oakum
kb: Loose fiber rope driven into seams and sealed with pitch
note: Oakum is unraveled rope fiber. Sailors drive it into seams with mallets and chisels, then seal over with tar. Leaks can be caulked at sea. The kernel is that the seam must be sealed from both sides, or water seeps past the caulking; hulls have internal seams that must also be caulked after the hull is built.

name: Bilge pump
kb: Hand-operated pump removing water from the hold
note: Bilge pump is a simple piston pump with flapper valves. Two sailors working alternately can keep a large ship dry. The kernel is that a ship always leaks; a crew must pump continuously during a long voyage. Without pumping, a wooden ship sinks in weeks.

name: Watertight bulkhead
kb: Internal wall extending from keel to deck sealing compartments
note: Bulkheads divide the hull into compartments; if one leaks, the ship does not sink immediately. Requires bulkheads to be truly watertight; any opening (door, pipe) must have a tight closure. The kernel is that a single leak in the lowest compartment sinks a ship; bulkheads buy time for repairs or evacuation.

name: Double bottom hull structure
kb: Inner hull separated from outer hull by empty space
note: Double bottom provides flotation even if the outer hull is punctured. Also allows water ballast without contaminating cargo. The kernel is that this doubles the weight and construction cost, but dramatically improves safety and cargo flexibility.

name: Iron hull construction
kb: Wrought iron frames and plates riveted into a hull
note: Iron hulls are stronger than wooden hulls; iron does not rot. Riveted seams work but require enormous labor. The kernel is that iron hulls can be larger and thinner-walled than wooden hulls, and a shipyard can build multiple copies if frames are reused. Initial capital investment is high.

name: Steel hull construction
kb: Bulk steel frames and plates for much stronger hulls
note: Steel is stronger than iron; hulls can be thinner and faster. Requires bulk steel production at scale. The kernel is that welded seams (instead of rivets) are superior, but welding came late; early steel hulls still used rivets. Transition from iron to steel hulls took decades.

name: Riveted hull plating
kb: Iron plate seams joined by driven rivets
note: Rivets are heated red-hot, inserted through holes in overlapping plates, then hammered cold on the far side. Requires enormous labor and skill. The kernel is that a poorly driven rivet pulls water in; a perfect rivet creates a watertight joint. Modern riveting uses pneumatic hammers, earlier work is all hand hammering and is exhausting.

name: Welded hull seams
kb: Electric arc welding of hull plate seams
note: Welded seams are stronger than riveted and save labor. Early welded hulls had fatigue cracks in service; design must avoid stress concentrations. The kernel is that riveted seams leak gradually, welded seams either work or fail suddenly. Transition from rivets to welds required understanding fatigue.

name: Screw propeller
kb: Archimedean screw submerged in water pushing ship forward
note: Screw propeller is more efficient than paddle wheel in rough seas, but requires shaft alignment that paddle wheels do not. The kernel is that any misalignment creates vibration that damages bearings. Modern propellers use bronze casting and careful balancing.

name: Paddle wheel for propulsion
kb: Large wheel with paddles pushing water astern
note: Paddle wheels are simple but inefficient; they throw water up as well as back. Efficiency is worse in rough seas where paddles lose water contact. The kernel is that paddle wheels project far above the deck, limiting gun ports and cargo space. Screw propellers fit inside the hull.

name: Variable pitch propeller
kb: Propeller blades rotating on boss to change pitch angle
note: Variable pitch blades allow reversing without reversing engine rotation. Requires oil pressure or mechanical linkage to operate. The kernel is that this is complex and reliable operation needs careful maintenance; fixed-pitch propellers are simpler and still common.

name: Stern tube and stuffing box
kb: Bearing tube in hull supporting propeller shaft with watertight seal
note: Stern tube is a bronze or iron tube through the hull; the propeller shaft rotates inside. Stuffing box at the hull side has packing that compresses to seal water out. The kernel is that the seal must allow the shaft to rotate freely, yet not leak; packing material (cotton or asbestos impregnated) is compressed progressively.

name: Marine steam engine
kb: Compact steam engine adapted for continuous ship propulsion
note: Marine engines are much more compact than stationary engines and must run continuously at sea. Crankshaft is horizontal, connected directly to the propeller shaft. The kernel is that connecting a steam engine to a propeller requires a strong crankshaft on good bearings; vibration at full power tests the bearings.

name: Triple expansion marine engine
kb: Three cylinders: high, intermediate, and low pressure
note: Three stages of expansion extract more work from steam. Complex coordination of cylinders; triple expansion engines were the workhorse of ocean freight.

name: Water tube boiler
kb: Tubes carrying water surrounded by hot gases
note: Water tube boilers have tubes in a furnace, opposite of locomotive boilers. More efficient steam generation than fire-tube boilers.

name: Marine steam turbine
kb: Rotary turbine directly driven by steam pressure
note: Turbines operate at high speeds; rotor must be perfectly balanced. Requires reduction gearing to run propeller at usable speed.

name: Reduction gearing for propeller
kb: Gears reducing turbine speed to optimal propeller speed
note: Turbines spin 3000+ rpm; propellers need 100-300 rpm. Reduction gears convert speed and torque. The kernel is that gear teeth must be precisely machined and case-hardened; poor gearing efficiency losses appear as heat in the gear case.

name: Marine diesel engine
kb: Diesel engine adapted for marine propulsion
note: Marine diesels are much larger and slower-running than automotive diesels. Direct drive to the propeller is possible. Efficiency is superior to steam turbines. The kernel is that marine diesel fuel (bunker oil) is heavy and requires heating before injection; fuel systems are complex.

name: Ballast tank system
kb: Sea water ballast tanks controlling ship trim and stability
note: Ballast tanks allow a ship to adjust its weight distribution without cargo. Ballast is seawater pumped in or out through gates. The kernel is that ballast must be carefully distributed; uneven ballast causes the ship to heel dangerously. Ballast tanks also allow ships to carry cargo efficiently despite variable load.

name: Submarine pressure hull
kb: Strong cylindrical hull withstanding deep water pressure
note: Submarine hulls must be round to distribute pressure evenly; any flat section risks catastrophic collapse. Riveting was unreliable at deep pressure; early submarines were limited to shallow depth. The kernel is that this requires bulk steel, perfect riveting or welding, and careful design of openings.

name: Periscope
kb: Optical tube with mirrors allowing viewing from submerged position
note: Periscope tube has lenses at top and bottom, mirror or prism in center. Light path bends 90 degrees at each end. The kernel is that mirror quality determines image brightness; tarnished mirrors make the image dim and hard to use in darkness.

name: Lifeboat and davit system
kb: Small boat stowed on ship with crane for emergency evacuation
note: Lifeboats must be strong enough for occupants, yet light enough to hoist with hand-cranked davits. Canvas or cork flotation prevents swamping. The kernel is that early lifeboats were poorly designed; many people drowned in lifeboats that swamped. Modern designs have watertight compartments and proper freeboard.

name: Ship telegraph signal system
kb: Telegraph link from bridge to engine room for speed commands
note: Telegraph is a mechanical system using electromagnets; a bell rings in the engine room when the bridge operator moves a lever. Modern engine rooms are out of earshot; telegraph eliminated the need for runners. The kernel is that the bridge can command engine speed directly, improving maneuverability.

name: Gyrocompass repeater
kb: Repeater display of gyro bearing fed electrically from master gyro
note: Gyrocompass master is large and fixed; repeaters on the bridge show bearing without leaving the compass. Multiple repeaters feed from one master. The kernel is that synchronizing repeaters with the master requires feedback mechanisms; errors accumulate if not corrected.

name: Log and sounding instruments
kb: Log line for speed, lead line with marks for depth
note: Log line is a rope with knots at regular intervals; tossed overboard, the knots passing a sailor's hand count the ship speed in knots. Sounding line is weighted and marked in fathoms. The kernel is that depth and speed are essential for navigation; old technology works reliably.

name: Lighthouse and Fresnel lens
kb: Stepped glass lens concentrating light into a beam
note: Fresnel lens steps the surface instead of grinding a smooth lens; this reduces weight and glass volume. Efficiency is excellent, throwing light far out to sea. The kernel is that stepped surfaces are precise optical elements; the step geometry must be calculated carefully or the beam disperses.

name: Dry dock facility
kb: Large dock that can be filled with water then drained
note: Dry dock allows hull repair below the waterline. Massive gates and pumping systems. The kernel is that the gates must seal perfectly; any leakage fills the dock and sinks the ship. Construction is expensive and takes years.

name: Slipway for ship launch
kb: Inclined ramp for sliding finished ship into water
note: Ship slides down the slipway into water. Friction is controlled by grease and soap. The kernel is that the angle and friction must be calculated correctly; too steep and the ship accelerates uncontrollably, too shallow and it sticks halfway.

name: Canal lock for water level control
kb: Pair of gates with pump or natural flow controlling water level
note: Locks allow boats to navigate waterfalls or height differences. Gates must seal perfectly; any leak drains the lock. The kernel is that operating a lock requires skill: chambers must be filled and drained at the right rate, and gates must close in sequence or water escapes.

name: Canal lift water elevator
kb: Large tank lift carrying boats vertically up or down
note: Canal lift replaces a series of locks with a single vertical motion. Large tank holds the boat; steam engine or counterweight lifts it. The kernel is that this is mechanically complex and rarely used; locks are simpler and more reliable. Only justified where height difference is extreme.

name: Dredger for channel deepening
kb: Boat with steam-driven pump or bucket dredge
note: Dredgers remove silt and mud from channels. Bucket dredge uses a belt-driven scoop; suction dredge uses a pump and pipeline. The kernel is that sediment is abrasive; pump impellers and bucket liners wear out quickly and require frequent replacement.

name: Tug boat for towing
kb: Small powerful boat for towing large cargo vessels
note: Tugs are high-powered relative to size; maneuverability is essential for harbor work. Engine and boiler dominate the design; cargo space is minimal. The kernel is that tugs must generate high torque at low speed to pull; reduction gearing or direct-drive low-speed engines are used.

name: Brake shoe on wheels
kb: Cast iron shoe pressed against wheel rim by brake lever
note: Early brakes used wooden shoes; cast iron shoes are more durable. The kernel is that shoe friction converts kinetic energy to heat; excessive braking overheats shoes and reduces friction.

name: Axle bearing journal box
kb: Cast iron housing containing brass or bronze bushing
note: Bearing box contains the bushing that carries the axle. Must have drain hole for oil leakage; a clogged box overheats. The kernel is that hot boxes derail trains; inspection and re-oiling on schedule is essential maintenance.

name: Smoke box and char arrester
kb: Chamber above boiler tubes collecting exhaust gases
note: Smoke box is a chamber where all tubes exit. Char arrester is a mesh inside; sparks are caught so they do not ignite lineside crops. The kernel is that locomotive operation without a spark arrester sets fires; railroads are liable for fire damage.

name: Grade crossing and safety gates
kb: Road crossing railroad at ground level with mechanical gates
note: Grade crossing gates lower mechanically when a train approaches; must be reliable or collisions occur. The kernel is that gate timing must be exact; gates must lower before the train reaches the crossing and raise after it clears.

name: Standard rail gauge
kb: Standardized track width allowing interchange between railroads
note: Many early railroads used different gauges; passengers had to change trains. Standardization on 4ft 8.5in allowed through-travel. The kernel is that this was a political achievement, not a technical one; railroads had to agree to lose the monopoly on traffic.

name: Sextant for celestial navigation
kb: Double-mirror instrument measuring angles to celestial bodies
note: Sextant has two mirrors and a half-silvered beam-splitter. User sees the horizon and celestial body simultaneously, then measures the angle. The kernel is that accuracy depends on optical clarity and mechanical precision; a sextant made with care is accurate to 1 minute of arc.

name: Marine chronometer for longitude
kb: Highly accurate clock keeping time during voyage for longitude calculation
note: Chronometers use a balance wheel and hairspring in a gimbal mount. Temperature compensation is critical; expansion changes spring rate and loses time. The kernel is that a simple spring-driven watch gains and loses seconds per day, but a chronometer must lose less than one second per month.

name: Mast stepping and rigging
kb: Method for setting masts and distributing load through ship structure
note: Masts are large wooden poles; stepping is the joint between mast and hull. Must be strong enough to carry both the sail load and bending moments. The kernel is that mast failure means loss of ship; stepped joint design evolved through centuries of trial and failure.

name: Fore-and-aft rigging system
kb: Network of shrouds, stays, and halyards controlling sails
note: Fore-and-aft rigging has many lines: shrouds hold the mast, stays are forward-backward lines, halyards raise sails. Each line serves a specific purpose. The kernel is that a single failed line can drop the mast; rigging must be redundant and sailors must know which lines to splice.

name: Keelson internal keel
kb: Longitudinal timber glued to top of keel inside the hull
note: Keelson is sandwiched between the keel and the frames, glued and bolted. Reinforces longitudinal strength. The kernel is that hogging is prevented; without a keelson, large wooden ships flex and eventually break in half.

name: Internal hull sheathing and ceiling
kb: Interior planking protecting cargo from bilge water and hull moisture
note: Hull ceiling is laid over the frames on the inside. Creates an air gap between cargo and hull structure. The kernel is that this requires careful carpentry to fit perfectly; gaps allow rot to spread.

name: Bowsprit extension spar
kb: Spar extending forward from bow supporting jibs
note: Bowsprit is a large spar lashed to the bow, extending 10-40 feet. Jibs hang from it. The kernel is that the bowsprit is in compression from the jib load and tension from lashing; if the lashing fails, the bowsprit falls and often takes the foremast with it.

name: Block rigging and rope lashing
kb: Splicing and knotting techniques for rope connections
note: A badly spliced rope breaks under load; a properly spliced rope retains 80 percent of rope strength. The kernel is that this is craft knowledge passed sailmaker to sailmaker; a perfect splice is invisible and stronger than the line on either side.
